turns.prompt_text: I've got another microwave that's been sitting for a few weeks I'm pretty sure I need to take a multimeter to test this to ensure it doesn't have a lethal voltage before I try to clip the wires or pry them off Attached 1 file. - 110513e5-f9fa-4ea8-a508-ead4f6dd5262
turns.response_html:
⚠️ Stop! Do Not Rely on a Multimeter First

Your instinct to treat this with extreme caution is spot-on—microwave high-voltage capacitors can store thousands of volts and are easily the most dangerous component inside the appliance.

However, using a standard multimeter to test for voltage before discharging is unsafe:

  • Voltage Limitations: Standard multimeters and test leads are typically rated up to $600\text{ V}$ or $1000\text{ V}$ (CAT II/III). Microwave capacitors operate at around $2,000\text{ V}$ to $2,500\text{ V}$ and store high-voltage DC. Attempting to measure a live HV capacitor with standard probes can cause internal arcing, flashover, or destroy the meter.
  • Internal Bleed Resistors Can Fail: The schematic printed on your capacitor label (the resistor symbol labeled 10MΩ) indicates an internal bleed resistor designed to drain charge. However, bleed resistors can fail open, leaving a lethal charge intact even after the microwave has been sitting for weeks.

The Safe Procedure: Discharge First

You must physically discharge the capacitor before touching, clipping, or pulling off any wires.

Step-by-Step Discharge

  1. Unplug the Appliance: Ensure there is no connection to wall power.
  2. Use an Insulated Tool: Grab a screwdriver with a thick, undamaged rubber or plastic insulated handle.
  3. One-Hand Rule: Keep your non-working hand behind your back or in your pocket to prevent creating a current path across your chest.
  4. Ground to Chassis First: Place the metal shaft of the screwdriver firmly against the unpainted metal chassis frame of the microwave.
  5. Short the Terminals: While keeping the screwdriver shaft in solid contact with the metal frame, slide the blade over to touch one terminal post, then the second terminal post, and finally bridge directly across both terminal posts simultaneously.
  6. Hold for a Few Seconds: Hold contact for 3 to 5 seconds across all points. If any residual charge was present, you might hear a loud pop or see a spark.

Verifying with a Multimeter

Only after you have manually shorted both terminals to each other and to the bare metal chassis is it safe to touch the terminals or use a multimeter. At that point, you can safely use your meter to test the capacitor's resistance or capacitance without risk of high-voltage shock or meter damage.
